UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC
                                    Docket No. CP26-25-000


 FOURTH SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF JUSTIN KULOVSEK, REQUESTING
    SUPPLEMENTAL DATA REQUESTS, ADDITIONAL NEPA REVIEW, AND
          ADDRESSING PUBLIC CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY


                                       Filed: June 25, 2026



                                      I. INTRODUCTION
Justin Kulovsek, a landowner whose property at 7350 Flemingsburg Road, Morehead, Kentucky
40351 (Rowan County parcels KY-RO-044.000 and KY-RO-043.000) lies at approximately
Milepost 4.25 of the proposed Maysville Pipeline route, respectfully submits these Fourth
Supplemental Comments as a pro se intervenor in the above-captioned proceeding pursuant to
Rules 211 and 214 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. sections
385.211 and 385.214.
These comments are the fourth filing Intervenor has submitted in response to Columbia Gulf
Transmission, LLC's (Columbia Gulf) data request response filed June 23, 2026 (Accession No.
20260623-5110). They also incorporate findings from EPIC Report No. 2026-001, Data Centers
in Kentucky: Policy Analysis for the General Assembly, published by the Kentucky Energy
Planning and Inventory Commission (EPIC) in June 2026 pursuant to KRS 164.2807. EPIC is a
Kentucky state agency created by the General Assembly to provide independent analysis of
energy supply adequacy, rate design, and infrastructure planning. The EPIC Report provides
independent confirmation, from a state agency with expertise in Kentucky energy markets, of the
cost causation and ratepayer protection concerns this proceeding raises.
Intervenor respectfully submits that the materials now before the Commission present a
substantially stronger basis for supplemental data requests before a certificate is issued than
existed when this proceeding began.



          II. THE CAPACITY GAP IN COLUMBIA GULF'S SWORN FILINGS
The Maysville Pipeline Project is designed for 340,000 Dekatherms per day (Dth/day) of
capacity. The stated purpose is to supply natural gas to East Kentucky Power Cooperative's
 (EKPC) Spurlock Station in Mason County for a coal-to-gas co-firing retrofit, with commercial
operation in December 2029.
Columbia Gulf's fuel study (Attachment A, filed June 23, 2026, under oath, Accession No.
20260623-5110) confirms the following sworn project parameters:


Parameter                                        Columbia Gulf Filed Value
Pipeline Capacity                                340,000 Dth/day
Load Factor Used                                 75%
Annual Throughput at 75% CF                      93,075,000 Dth/year (255,000 Dth/day average)
Installed Horsepower                             0 hp
Estimated Fuel Gas                               0 Dth/day
Project Company Use Gas Rate                     0.000%
Quantified Benefit to Existing Customers         -0.249% retainage reduction (3.168% to
                                                 2.919%)


Standard engineering calculation using published EKPC data establishes that Spurlock Station at
its maximum co-firing parameters (50% gas co-fire, 75% capacity factor, subcritical heat rate of
approximately 10,200 BTU/kWh) requires approximately 123,000 Dth/day. At 100% capacity
factor with 50% co-fire, the upper bound reaches approximately 164,000 Dth/day, which is 48%
of the pipeline's 340,000 Dth/day design capacity.
Columbia Gulf's own sworn filing projects 255,000 Dth/day average throughput at the 75% load
factor it chose for analysis. That figure is 91,000 Dth/day above Spurlock Station's maximum co-
firing requirement. The record contains no explanation for this gap. Additionally, the fuel study's
representation of 0 hp compression and 0 Dth/day fuel gas for a 340,000 Dth/day, 42-mile, 1,440
psi pipeline has not been independently verified and warrants engineering review.



III. THE DATA CENTER DEMAND: PUBLIC DISCLOSURES AND STATE AGENCY
                         CONFIRMATION
Intervenor has previously identified in the FERC record that EKPC publicly disclosed that a
Fortune 100 company is constructing a hyperscale data center in Mason County, Kentucky, with
power delivery beginning December 2026 at 110 megawatts and scaling to 2,200 megawatts by
2031. EKPC obtained a special Data Center Power Tariff from the Kentucky Public Service
Commission in October 2025. In the Matter of the Electronic Tariff Filing of East Kentucky
Power Cooperative, Inc. to Establish a New Tariff for Data Center Power, Order, Case No. 2025-
00140, Ky. P.S.C. Oct. 30, 2025.
 EPIC Report No. 2026-001, published June 2026 pursuant to KRS 164.2807, provides
independent confirmation from a Kentucky state agency of the scale of data center development
in EKPC's service territory. The EPIC Report identifies the following directly relevant findings:


       First: EKPC currently has 11 active data center projects seeking over 10 gigawatts of
       power. The 2,200 MW Mason County project is one of eleven. This is not a single
       isolated customer commitment; it is a pattern of large-load development concentrated in
       EKPC's service territory that is not reflected in the Maysville Pipeline's public need
       justification as filed.


       Second: Mason County is specifically identified in the EPIC Report as a county with data
       center projects under active consideration. This independently corroborates Intervenor's
       prior analysis connecting the Maysville Pipeline's terminus location to the data center
       demand profile documented in EKPC's public filings.


       Third: The EPIC Report confirms that EKPC's Data Center Power Tariff (Case No.
       2025-00140) was designed to ensure the customer bears the full cost of infrastructure it
       directly causes. The EPIC Report articulates the broader cost causation principle: costs
       should be assigned to the customer whose service requirements produce them. However,
       the EPIC Report's analysis is limited to electric utility infrastructure. It does not address
       natural gas pipeline infrastructure costs.


       Fourth: The EPIC Report explicitly acknowledges that FERC-jurisdictional costs fall
       outside the scope of the PSC's direct authority, stating that retail tariff structures
       approved by the PSC cannot override FERC-jurisdictional regional cost allocation rules.
       Natural gas pipeline infrastructure approved through FERC's Section 7(c) certificate
       process is precisely this category of cost.


This creates a material gap in the cost causation framework the EPIC Report otherwise endorses.
Even if EKPC's Data Center Power Tariff requires the data center customer to pay for the gas-
fired generation EKPC constructs to serve it, the cost of the Maysville Pipeline itself flows
through Columbia Gulf's FERC-approved transportation rates to EKPC as a gas shipper, and
from there into EKPC's fuel and purchased power costs. Those costs are recovered through
EKPC's standard cooperative rate mechanisms, not through the Data Center Power Tariff.
EKPC's approximately 1.1 million member-customers would bear those costs.
The EPIC Report reinforces why this matters particularly for electric cooperatives. As the Report
observes, for member-owned cooperatives there is no external shareholder buffer: if costs are
disallowed or market outcomes weaken cooperative financial metrics, the residual risk remains
within the cooperative system and is ultimately borne by member-owners, who are also the end-
 use customers. The EPIC Report further documents the broader infrastructure cost risk
environment: PJM capacity clearing prices rose from $28.92 per megawatt-day in the 2024/25
auction to $333.44 per megawatt-day in the 2027/28 auction, a nearly 12-fold increase over three
years. Ohio's AEP imposed an 85% minimum billing floor and 12-year contract terms to curb
speculative large-load requests. Virginia utilities face projected residential rate increases of $14
to $37 per month by 2040.
The EPIC Report also identifies FERC Docket RM26-4-000, a large-load interconnection
rulemaking in which the Commission has committed to act by the end of June 2026. FERC is
already examining the infrastructure cost allocation implications of large-load growth at the
transmission level. The same cost causation question presents itself at the gas pipeline level in
this proceeding.
Standard engineering calculation using a combined-cycle gas turbine heat rate of approximately
7,200 BTU/kWh establishes that supplying 2,200 megawatts of generation at 75% capacity
factor requires approximately 285,000 Dth/day. At 100% capacity factor, the requirement
approaches 380,000 Dth/day. The Maysville Pipeline's design capacity of 340,000 Dth/day falls
squarely within that range.



          IV. THE SOLE QUANTIFIED PUBLIC BENEFIT IS INSUFFICIENT
Columbia Gulf's sworn fuel study identifies a single quantified benefit to the public: a 0.249
percentage-point reduction in mainline gas retainage for existing Columbia Gulf customers, from
the current 3.168% combined system rate established in the Columbia Gulf 2026 Rate
Adjustment Mechanism Filing (Docket RP26-559-000, accepted March 24, 2026) to a projected
2.919% combined post-project rate.
This is the evidentiary basis on which the Commission is asked to issue a certificate authorizing
eminent domain over private landowners' property in Rowan, Fleming, and Mason Counties
under Section 7(h) of the Natural Gas Act, 15 U.S.C. section 717f(h). To authorize eminent
domain over rural Kentucky landowners on the basis of a 0.249 percentage-point retainage
reduction, while the primary capacity beneficiary of the pipeline remains undisclosed behind a
non-disclosure agreement, is precisely the outcome FERC's certificate policy standards were
designed to prevent.
FERC's 1999 Certificate Policy Statement, 88 FERC para. 61,227, requires the Commission to
weigh project benefits against the interests of existing customers and affected landowners. The
2022 interim Updated Certificate Policy Statement (Docket PL18-1) requires examination of the
end-use of capacity. The EPIC Report's articulation of the cost causation principle reinforces this
framework: if the primary service requirement driving this pipeline's sizing is a 2,200 MW data
center load and associated generation, that customer should bear the associated infrastructure
costs. FERC should require the record to reflect that determination before a certificate issues.
                       V. NEPA AND DOWNSTREAM EMISSIONS

The environmental assessment for this project was scoped to analyze the stated purpose: natural
     gas supply to Spurlock Station's coal-to-gas co-firing program. If the pipeline is sized
substantially to serve gas-fired generation associated with data center demand in Mason County
 or elsewhere in EKPC's service territory, the downstream greenhouse gas emissions from that
                                   generation were not assessed.
The D.C. Circuit held in Sabal Trail Transmission, LLC, 867 F.3d 1357, 1373-74 (D.C. Cir.
2017), that FERC must assess reasonably foreseeable downstream environmental effects in its
NEPA review of natural gas pipeline projects, including greenhouse gas emissions from gas
combustion at end-use facilities. If this pipeline supplies gas to combined-cycle generation
EKPC constructs to serve the Mason County data center or any of the 10 other active data center
projects in EKPC's service territory identified in the EPIC Report, those emissions are the
reasonably foreseeable downstream consequence of this project and must be analyzed before a
certificate is issued.



                                VI. SPECIFIC REQUESTS
Based on the foregoing, Intervenor respectfully requests that the Commission take the
following actions before issuing a certificate of public convenience and necessity:


       1. Require Columbia Gulf and EKPC to produce all precedent agreements, letters of
       intent, and contingent contracts related to any electric generation facility or large
       industrial customer that would use natural gas supplied by the Maysville Pipeline,
       including any generation built to serve the Mason County data center and any of the 11
       active data center projects identified in EPIC Report No. 2026-001.


       2. Commission or require independent hydraulic analysis verifying that a 340,000
       Dth/day, 42-mile, 30-inch, 1,440 psi pipeline can be constructed and operated with 0
       horsepower of installed compression and 0 Dth/day of fuel gas as stated in Columbia
       Gulf's sworn fuel study (Attachment A, Accession No. 20260623-5110).


       3. Require Columbia Gulf and EKPC to disclose the end-use of the pipeline's capacity
       above Spurlock Station co-firing requirements, including whether any capacity is
       designated, contracted, or otherwise committed to serve gas-fired generation associated
       with the Mason County data center or any other data center project in EKPC's service
       territory identified in the EPIC Report.


       4. Expand the NEPA scope of review to assess the reasonably foreseeable downstream
       greenhouse gas emissions from all natural gas combustion supplied by this pipeline,
        including emissions from any combined-cycle generation EKPC constructs to serve data
       center demand, consistent with Sabal Trail Transmission, LLC, 867 F.3d 1357 (D.C. Cir.
       2017).


       5. Condition any certificate of public convenience and necessity on a finding that the
       pipeline's full capacity is allocated to end-uses satisfying the public convenience and
       necessity standard under Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act, 15 U.S.C. section 717f(c),
       and that the eminent domain authority conferred by Section 7(h) is not being used
       primarily to benefit a private industrial customer whose identity is protected from public
       disclosure by a non-disclosure agreement.



                                     VII. CONCLUSION
The record before the Commission now contains two independent bodies of evidence pointing to
the same gap. Columbia Gulf's own sworn fuel study confirms a pipeline sized well above
Spurlock Station's stated needs, projecting average throughput of 255,000 Dth/day against a
maximum co-firing requirement of approximately 164,000 Dth/day. EPIC Report No. 2026-001,
a June 2026 publication of a Kentucky state agency charged by statute with independent energy
infrastructure analysis, confirms that EKPC has over 10 gigawatts of active data center load,
including projects in Mason County, that are driving infrastructure commitments not currently
visible in this FERC proceeding.
EPIC's core principle applies directly here: cost allocation rules must be in place before
infrastructure is built, and costs should be assigned to the customer whose service requirements
produce them. The natural gas pipeline cost is the one component of EKPC's data center
infrastructure supply chain that falls outside the PSC's jurisdiction and squarely within FERC's.
FERC has already acknowledged, through its RM26-4-000 rulemaking, that large-load growth
raises serious infrastructure cost allocation questions at the transmission level. The same
question presents itself here, at the gas pipeline level.
The record does not currently answer who this pipeline is primarily for. The Commission
has the authority, and Intervenor respectfully submits the obligation, to obtain that answer
before issuing a certificate that makes the question effectively unreviewable.

Respectfully submitted,




Justin Kulovsek
Intervenor, Pro Se
7350 Flemingsburg Road
Morehead, Kentucky 40351
